meta.title: Driving after Epilepsy Surgery — COSY for auras only vs seizure-free
meta.authors: Fairclough S, O'Keeffe AG, de Tisi J, Duncan JS
meta.outcome: Chance of a seizure with impaired awareness in the next 12 months (COSY) after epilepsy surgery, by the worst ILAE outcome grade over the previous 1, 2 or 3 years.
meta.clinical_utility: Driving counselling after epilepsy surgery, in particular for people who continue to have auras only.
meta.cff_info:
What this shows. The chance of a seizure with impaired awareness in the next 12 months (COSY) for a person who has had epilepsy surgery, given the worst seizure outcome over the last 1, 2 or 3 years (Fairclough et al., J Neurol Neurosurg Psychiatry 2018). Its main question is whether people who still have auras only (focal aware seizures) after surgery have a risk comparable with people who are completely seizure-free.

Cohort. 819 patients operated at the National Hospital for Neurology and Neurosurgery, London, between 1990 and 2014, followed for 2–25 years (mean 11.4), 9307 patient-years in total. 77% had a temporal lobectomy; the commonest pathology was hippocampal sclerosis (61%). Every post-operative year was graded prospectively on the ILAE surgery-outcome scale.

Method. The estimates come from generalised estimating equations (logistic, robust standard errors), so the 95% confidence intervals account for the same patient contributing many years. Time since surgery did not change the risk (odds ratio 1.00 per year, 0.99–1.02).

Key findings

  • Seizure-free (ILAE 1) for 1, 2 and 3 years: COSY 4.9%, 3.5% and 2.4%.
  • Auras only (ILAE 2) for 1, 2 and 3 years: COSY 11.3%, 9.2% and 7.8% — higher than seizure-free, but the upper 95% limit stays well below 20% (14.0% at 1 year).
  • A seizure beyond auras (ILAE 3–6) in the last year: COSY 87.6%.

Limits. One specialist centre, and no external validation. Auras are self-reported and their frequency is often poorly recalled, so the auras-only group may be misclassified. The estimates are marginal: they do not adjust for patient factors such as pathology, antiseizure-medication changes or withdrawal. The 34 deaths (4.2%) were not modelled. Surgery took place 1990–2014.

Driving. The authors argue that, if a COSY below 20% is accepted for private driving, people with auras only after surgery could be allowed to drive. This is their proposal, not a licensing rule: at the time of publication UK rules did not allow it for anyone with a past seizure with impaired awareness. Local laws and guidelines apply.

predictors.name: Period considered
predictors.assess: How many of the most recent post-operative years to consider. The outcome below is the WORST grade in any of those years: 'last 2 years' with 'auras only' means no seizure beyond auras in either year and auras in at least one of them.

predictors.name: Worst outcome in that period
predictors.assess: ILAE epilepsy-surgery outcome scale, applied to each post-operative year. ILAE 1 = completely seizure-free, no auras. ILAE 2 = auras (focal seizures without impaired awareness) only. ILAE 3–6 = at least one seizure day beyond auras (3 = one to three seizure days a year; 4–6 = more). The paper pools grades 3–6 and treats them as seizures with impaired awareness.

chart.title: Every period and outcome, with 95% CI
chart.info: Each dot is the published COSY for one combination of period and worst outcome, with its 95% confidence interval as a bar. Dashed lines mark the 20% (private) and 2% (commercial) orientation cut-offs. Click a row to select it.
